catalog_quote: Ichishkiin has word level stress, with one primary stress per spoken word. Stress is indicated with raised pitch and greater intensity in the stressed syllable (Hargus and Beavert 2005). As noted above, a stress shift can change the meaning of a word, for example pámta, the address form for 'woman's brother's son' and pamtá 'bullfrog, toad'. [p. 52] ... Where the stress will fall in a root is not predictable. Any syllable of a root can be stressed. ... Although stress is not entirely predictable, there are some tendencies for where root stress will fall based on patterns of consonants (here abbreviated C) and vowels (V). ... Note though, there are exceptions to each of these tendencies. ... The tendencies can help language learners make guesses for stress placement, but ultimately where the stress belongs needs to be learned as part of a word. [p. 53] Some prefixes and suffixes are inherently stressed and will (almost always) receive the word level stress. I refer to these as 'stress-stealing' because they override the stress of the root they are attached to. [p. 54] ... The rule for stress assignment of a word is shown below, and is due to the work of Hargus and Beavert (2005, 2006b). In Figure 2.2 below, the morphemes to the left overcome the stress of morphemes to their right. FIGURE 2.2. STRESS ASSIGNMENT: stress-stealing suffix > strong root > stress-stealing prefix > root [p. 56]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: yaki1237 (Northwest Sahaptin, Yakima dialect) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Hargus & Beavert 2005 (UWWPL 24: 64-95), was previously recorded as unobtainable;washington.edu/uwwpl/vol24/; ResearchWorks only holds UWWPL 2020-2024), downloaded and read it, saved PDF + text under and updated. It is the first-hand statement of record: one culminative primary stress per word, lexically unpredictable within roots (near-minimal pairs), statistical preferences for heavy syllables / initial in CVCV / penult in CVCVCV, lexically accented vs unaccented morphemes with outermost-suffix > outermost-prefix > root resolution, pitch + energy correlates, classified by the authors as pitch accent. Jansen 2010 §2.6 (held by the project) repeats the same picture citing this paper. If the language is added, suggested coding is lexical (morphological resolution; authors' label pitch accent). Nothing left to acquire for this item

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word has exactly one primary stress, realized as high pitch plus greater intensity. Within a root the stressed syllable is lexically specified (any syllable; only tendencies: initial in CVCV/CVCCV, heavy CVV/CVC syllables attract it, barred-i rarely stressed, each with counterexamples). Affixes are lexically accented ('stress-stealing', 43% of affixes) or unaccented; when a word contains several accented morphemes the surface stress is decided morphologically: an accented suffix beats a 'strong root', which beats an accented prefix, which beats an ordinary root; among several accented prefixes the leftmost wins, among several accented suffixes the rightmost. Hargus & Beavert (2006, 2009, 2014, 2016) describe the same system as a lexical pitch accent system (H tone on the accented syllable, obligatoriness and culminativity hold).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Jansen: none stated ('one primary stress per spoken word'). Hargus & Beavert 2016 (AMP, pp. 3-6): secondary stress (greater energy, no pitch peak) found only in trisyllabic-or-longer totally reduplicated iterative verbs, on the reduplicant and stem (e.g. [ilamájlaklamàjlakʃana]); disyllabic/monosyllabic reduplicated verbs show none; they cite Jacobs 1931:117 that Northwest Sahaptin words have 'only one syllable accented and no secondary stress' and reject Rude 1988's [k'ùsik'úsi] for Yakima ([k'usík'usi]).
new_statements.exceptions: Small class of 'strong roots' (e.g. tanawíix̱- 'argue', iwái- 'wait', tmaaní- 'pick berries') resist accented prefixes but not accented suffixes; stress varies by dialect (shushaynsh 'steelhead'); tendencies for root stress all have exceptions (luts'á 'red', tiichám 'land', kɨ́tu 'fast'); copula wa variably accented (H&B 2006). Unaccented function words and second-position clitics (ku 'and', uu 'or', =nash 1SG) carry no accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word including affixes; second-position clitics are unaccented and outside). Description is of the Yakima (Yakama) dialect from speaker Virginia Beavert; pitch-related interaction with sentence intonation (final L boundary tone blocked after accented short vowel) reported by Hargus & Beavert 2014/2016.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the Yakima (Yakama) dialect of Northwest Sahaptin, from speaker Virginia Beavert; Glottolog yaki1237 is the language-level code for Northwest Sahaptin (Yakima, Klikitat, Upper Cowlitz, etc.), so the description is dialect-specific within the target language. Jacobs 1931 (not opened) is mainly Klikitat, also Northwest. Rigsby & Rude 1996 and WALS 'Sahaptin (Umatilla)' (umat1237) are the River dialect, a different Glottolog language; Hargus & Beavert 2016 note Umatilla differs (multiple accented syllables per word per Jacobs).

new_statements.quote: In YS there are similar (near-)minimal pairs for stress; e.g. [wjánawi]- ‘arrive’, [anáwi]- ‘be hungry’, [kw’ajawí] ‘mountain lion’. In an earlier study (Hargus and Beavert 2001), we noted that despite such contrasts, there were nonetheless statistical preferences for stress placement in roots. There is a greater-than-random attraction of stress to heavy syllables (–VV or -VC), a preference for trochaic stress when syllable weight is not a factor (e.g. initial stress in CVCV roots), and a preference for right-directionality (penultimate stress in CVCVCV roots).
new_statements.citation: Hargus, Sharon & Virginia Beavert. 2005. A note on the phonetic correlates of stress in Yakima Sahaptin. University of Washington Working Papers in Linguistics 24: 64-95.
new_statements.locator: §3.1 'Unpredictability of Stress', pp. 65-66 (also §3.6 p. 76: 'there is one primary stress per word. When multiple morphemes with underlying stress coincide in the same word, stress is realized on the outermost suffix, then the outermost prefix, and then on the root.')
new_statements.reading: Yakima (Northwest) Sahaptin has one culminative primary stress per word whose position is lexically contrastive and unpredictable within roots (near-minimal pairs), with only statistical tendencies (heavy syllables attract stress; initial in CVCV; penultimate in CVCVCV); morphemes are lexically accented or not, and surface stress in complex words is resolved morphologically (outermost suffix > outermost prefix > root). Realized as high pitch + energy, not duration; the authors call it a pitch accent system. Catalog-style coding: lexical (with morphological resolution); authors' label tonal-OR-pitch accent. Consistent with Jansen 2010 §2.6 (pp. 52-55, already held by the project) which cites this paper and gives the same tendencies and stress-stealing affix rule.

new_statements.quote: Stress and high tone are one phenomenon in northern Sahaptin; they are very strongly marked in northwest Sahaptin. In the latter group, ordinary words have only one syllable accented and no secondary stress; freshly compounded words may have two equally stressed syllables [p. 117] ... In adverbs, particles and many nouns that are devoid of affixes, it seems impossible to determine rules for the presence of stress; accident, traditional usage, many unascertainable factors seem to have play. Wherever morphologic affixes are used, stress is governed rigidly by such grammatical factors. Definite rules may be formulated, based on the affixes present. [p. 118]

new_statements.rule_in_words: One accented syllable per ordinary word in northwest Sahaptin, no secondary stress; the accent is realized as high (short vowel) or falling (long vowel/diphthong) tone, i.e. stress and high tone are one phenomenon. In unaffixed words (adverbs, particles, many nouns) the position of stress follows no discoverable rule (lexical). Where affixes are present the position is fixed by the affixes: certain noun postpositions (-pama', -Gwa'k, -i'k, -ti'k, -(y)a'i, -(nə)mi') and certain verb prefixes/suffixes (a'-, pa'-, -i'k, -t, -a'c, -pama', -a'tad, and a list of prefixes/anterior roots on p. 119) always carry the word stress, with a precedence order (-pama' over all but possessive -mi'); otherwise 'the root is stressed if nothing else is stressed' and 'in most other cases in the verb, stress is on the initial syllable of the verb root complex'. Stress is contrastive only in the pa'- vs pa- homonyms (pa'wat'ana '(you) struck at me / hit him' vs pawa't'ana 'they struck at'). Monosyllabic words are always stressed with high tone except the proclitic connective ku-.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 117: 'ordinary words have only one syllable accented and no secondary stress; freshly compounded words may have two equally stressed syllables; these syllables seem felt as independent words from the point of view of stress.' p. 120: 'In northwest Sahaptin the only certain cases of coordinate stresses in words not compounds were in the verb forms iwa'tca', he was; pawa'tca', they were.' By contrast the Umatilla-reservation dialects (walu'la-palu's) allow two to four gentle accents per word (p. 117), with each verb root stressed (p. 120).
new_statements.exceptions: Unaffixed adverbs, particles and many nouns: no rule ('accident, traditional usage, many unascertainable factors'). Monosyllables unstressed in texts are treated as proclitics (connective ku- never stressed); the connectives a'uku'G / auku'k / a'uku etc. show unexplained variable stress (p. 117). Anterior root -qala- 'roll' is almost never accented (p. 119, exceptions cited p. 170). Pronouns: prefixed definite i'- always takes the accent, otherwise the first syllable of the pronoun root unless an accented suffix (-ni'ki, -ni'kin, -ni'n, -ə'k accusative, -a't'ca, -ksa', -kaya'i) is present; adverbs of manner from root verbs and reduplicated bisyllabic nouns are accented on the second syllable (p. 120). The final-verb past-tense -ya' accent and the penultimate-aspect rule (pp. 119-120) are stated for walu'la-palu's only, not for northwest Sahaptin.
new_statements.identity_note: Jacobs's 'Northern Sahaptin' covers two groups: northwest Sahaptin (xwa'lxwaipam Klikitat, ta'idnapam Upper Cowlitz, Yakima; informants Peter McGuff and Samson Quaempts for Klikitat, Sam N. Eyley Jr. of Morton, Lewis Co. for Upper Cowlitz with a Yakima father, pp. 97-98) and the Umatilla-reservation dialects walu'la-palu's (Walla Walla/Palouse) and yumati'la (Umatilla). The northwest-Sahaptin statements apply to yaki1237 (Glottolog Yakima = Northwest Sahaptin); the grammar's basic material is Upper Cowlitz/Klikitat rather than the Yakima proper described by Hargus & Beavert and Jansen. The walu'la-palu's stress statements (pp. 119-120) describe Walla Walla (wall1263) and do not bear on this language.

tone.quote: Stress in IS is culminative and obligatory within a morphological word, and it is phonetically cued by raised pitch and greater intensity on the stressed syllable (Hargus & Beavert 2005). The position of stress is generally phonologically unpredictable. As shown in Hargus & Beavert (2006; 2016) and Jansen (2010), both roots and afﬁxes (preﬁxes and sufﬁxes) can be underlyingly accented. Stress is contrastive, and minimal pairs can be found for morphemes (6), simplex words (7), and morphologically complex words as well (8)

tone.quote: Stress in IS is culminative and obligatory, and is phonetically cued by raised pitch and greater intensity in the stressed syllable (Hargus & Beavert 2005). Both roots and affixes (prefixes and suffixes) can be underlyingly accented. Hargus and Beavert (2001, 2006, 2016) claim that all roots in Ichishkiin are underlyingly accented, i.e. there are no words in the language which would not have an underlying accent.
